state school = a school funded by the government rather than by fees
independent school = a school funded by fees, not by the local authority
public school = in Britain, an old, expensive independent school
grammar school = a state secondary school that selects pupils by exam
comprehensive school = a state secondary school that takes pupils of all abilities
boarding school = a school where pupils live during term time
single-sex school = a school for only boys or only girls
co-educational school = a school that teaches boys and girls together
faith school = a school linked to a religion and its values
special school = a school for pupils with significant additional needs
vocational college = a college that trains students for a trade or practical career
sixth form = the last two years of secondary school, often for A-levels
further education = study after secondary school that is not a full university degree
academy school = a state-funded school in England that is independent of the local council
mixed-ability teaching = teaching pupils of different levels in the same class
academic streaming = putting pupils into classes by overall academic ability
school catchment area = the neighbourhood from which a school normally takes pupils
school fees = money paid to attend a private or independent school
selective school = a school that admits pupils by exam, interview or talent
compulsory education = the years when the law requires children to be in education
technical school = a secondary school that combines general study with a trade
humanities = subjects such as literature, history, philosophy and languages
social sciences = subjects that study people and society, such as sociology or economics
natural sciences = subjects such as physics, chemistry and biology
faculty = a large division of a university grouping related departments
academic department = a university unit that teaches and researches one subject
syllabus = an outline of topics, texts and assessment for a course
national curriculum = the official programme of study that state schools must follow
core subject = a subject all pupils must study, such as maths or the language of instruction
lecture = a formal talk teaching a group, typical at university
seminar = a small class for discussion of a topic or text
tutorial = a very small teaching session, often with one tutor and a few students
laboratory work = practical experiments done in a science lab as part of a course
geography fieldwork = research or practical study done outside the classroom, especially in geography
extra-curricular activity = a club or pursuit organised by the school but outside lessons
vocational training = practical preparation for a specific job or trade
interdisciplinary course = a course that combines methods from more than one subject
foundation course = a preparatory year before a full degree, often for a change of field
A-level = a British subject exam usually taken at eighteen for university entry
GCSE = a British subject exam usually taken at sixteen
International Baccalaureate = a two-year diploma programme recognised by universities worldwide
literacy = the ability to read and write at a functional level
numeracy = the ability to use numbers in everyday and work situations
information literacy = the skills needed to find, judge and use information, including online
admission requirements = the grades or qualifications needed to join a course
mock exam = a practice exam taken under real conditions before the official one
resit = a second attempt at an exam after a fail or a low grade
coursework = assessed work completed during a course rather than in a final exam
oral exam = a spoken test of knowledge or language
written examination = a formal test answered on paper or on screen
continuous assessment = grading based on work throughout the course, not one final paper
formative assessment = checking progress to improve learning, often without a final grade
summative assessment = a test or task that measures what has been learnt at the end of a unit
pass mark = the lowest score needed to succeed in a test
grade boundary = the score at which one grade changes to the next
academic transcript = an official record of modules and grades from an institution
credit points = units that measure the workload of a course or module
invigilator = a person who supervises an exam to prevent cheating
exam board = the organisation that sets and marks a public exam
marking criteria = the stated standards used to award marks
peer assessment = students judging one another's work against shared criteria
self-assessment = judging your own work or skills against a standard
open-book exam = a test in which you may use notes or textbooks
sit an exam = to take a formal test
distinction = the highest pass band on some courses and vocational awards
merit = a high pass band below distinction on some awards
appeal a grade = to formally ask for a mark to be reviewed
predicted grade = the result a teacher expects you to achieve in a public exam
school league table = a published ranking of schools by exam results
standardised test = an exam given in the same way so scores can be compared
oral presentation = a short spoken report, often with slides, assessed for content and delivery
fail a module = to not reach the pass mark for a unit of a course
conditional offer = a university place that depends on achieving set exam grades
clearing = the British process matching leftover university places to students after results
tuition fees = the money charged by a university for teaching
scholarship = money given to a student on merit or need to help pay for study
campus = the grounds and buildings of a university or college
undergraduate = a student studying for a first degree, or that level of study
postgraduate = a student studying after a first degree, or that level of study
dissertation = a long piece of original written work at the end of a degree
thesis = an extended research text, especially for a master's or doctorate
bachelor's degree = a first academic degree, typically after three or four years
master's degree = a higher degree taken after a bachelor's, often one or two years
PhD = the highest university degree, awarded for original research
fresher = a first-year university student in Britain
halls of residence = university buildings where students live, often in the first year
student loan = money borrowed to pay fees or living costs while studying
maintenance grant = non-repayable help towards a student's living costs
bursary = money given by a school or university, often according to need
mature student = a student who begins higher education later than the usual school-leaver age
distance learning = study done away from campus, typically online or by post
blended learning = a mix of face-to-face teaching and online study
open day = an event when prospective students visit and ask questions
prospectus = a brochure or site describing courses, facilities and entry rules
enrol = to officially register on a course or at an institution
lecture theatre = a large sloping room designed for lectures
academic year = the teaching year at a school or university, not the calendar year
sandwich course = a degree that includes a year of work in industry
exchange programme = an arrangement to study for a time at a partner institution abroad
vice-chancellor = the academic head of a British university
dean = the head of a faculty or a senior college officer
academic staff = the lecturers, professors and researchers employed by a university
research paper = a formal article presenting original findings
in-text citation = a brief reference in the body of a text pointing to a source
bibliography = the list of sources used in a piece of academic work
first-class honours = the highest UK bachelor's classification
joint honours = a degree that splits study equally between two subjects
foundation year = an extra preparatory year built into a degree for some students
alumni = former students of a school or university
graduation ceremony = the formal event at which degrees are conferred
students' union = the organisation that represents students and runs campus services
personal tutor = a member of staff assigned to support a student's academic progress
reading list = the books and articles a tutor expects you to study
office hours = published times when a lecturer is available to students
academic supervisor = the staff member who guides a dissertation or research project
viva voce = an oral examination, especially of a thesis
work placement = a period of supervised work that counts towards a course
UCAS = the central service through which students apply to UK universities
cram = to study intensively in a short time before a test
rote learning = memorising facts by repetition rather than by understanding
critical thinking = the skill of analysing arguments and evidence rather than accepting them
plagiarism = using someone else's words or ideas as if they were your own
gap year = a year out of formal study, often used to travel or work
drop out = to leave a course before finishing it
skip classes = to miss lessons without permission
brush up on = to improve knowledge of something you used to know better
fall behind = to progress more slowly than the course or your peers
catch up = to reach the required level after being behind
knuckle down = to start working seriously and with discipline
skim-read = to read quickly for the main points rather than every word
mind map = a diagram of ideas branching from a central topic
autonomous learner = a student who can plan, monitor and evaluate their own study
constructive feedback = comments that explain how work can be improved, not only what is wrong
time management = planning study and rest so deadlines are met without last-minute panic
procrastinate = to delay work that should be done now
study group = a small set of students who revise or solve problems together
past paper = an exam paper from a previous session, used for practice
academic integrity = honesty in study, including proper citation and no cheating
cite sources = to name the works you have used in academic writing
paraphrase = to rewrite an idea in your own words while keeping the meaning
proofread = to check a text for errors before submitting it
word limit = the maximum (and sometimes minimum) number of words allowed
abstract = a short summary of a paper or dissertation placed at the start
special educational needs = learning difficulties or disabilities that require extra support in school
dyslexia = a difficulty with reading and spelling that is not due to low intelligence
gifted pupil = a school student whose ability is well above the typical level
underachieve = to do less well than your ability suggests
inclusive education = schooling that educates pupils with diverse needs in ordinary settings where possible
mainstream school = an ordinary school, as opposed to a specialist separate setting
truancy = the habit of staying away from school without permission
learning outcomes = the knowledge and skills a course claims students will gain
scaffolding = temporary help that is withdrawn as the learner becomes able to work alone
supply teacher = a teacher who covers classes when the regular teacher is absent
teaching assistant = a member of staff who supports the teacher and individual pupils
head of department = the teacher in charge of a subject area in a school
newly qualified teacher = a teacher in the first year after gaining qualified teacher status
classroom management = the skills of organising behaviour and attention so that teaching can happen
permanent exclusion = removing a pupil from the school roll as a last disciplinary step
suspension = a temporary ban from attending school as a punishment
education reform = a planned change to how schools, exams or funding work
teacher shortage = a lack of qualified staff to fill teaching posts
class size = the number of pupils taught together in one group
flipped classroom = a method where students study content at home and practise in class
inquiry-based learning = a method in which pupils investigate questions rather than only receiving facts
e-learning = study that uses digital platforms as the main medium
MOOC = a free or low-cost online course open to very large numbers of learners
lifelong learning = continuing to study and retrain throughout adult life
adult education = organised learning for people who have left full-time school
continuing professional development = ongoing training that keeps practitioners' skills up to date
learner-centred = designed around students' needs and activity rather than only the teacher's talk
educational inequality = unfair differences in access, quality or outcomes of schooling
attainment gap = the difference in exam results between groups of pupils
homework gap = unequal ability to study at home because of missing devices, internet or space
disadvantaged background = growing up with fewer financial, educational or social resources
elite education = schooling that is highly selective, expensive or socially exclusive
school funding = the money provided to run schools, from the state or other sources
widening participation = policies that help under-represented groups enter higher education
private tuition = paid one-to-one or small-group teaching outside school
dropout rate = the share of students who leave a course before finishing
pupil premium = extra state money in England for schools with disadvantaged pupils
